If you have a good product marketing organization, good product marketing organization generally is very concerned with the positioning and the pitch, and those two things sit in their purview, but depends on how you define it. I can't wait till you get Airbnb. Tell us how this stuff works. They're different because they're a consumer, but companies are arranged in all different ways. So if you have product marketing, it looks one way. If you don't, it looks another way. Somebody's got to kind of be the owner of this thing though. And so we have to decide who that's going to be.
turns.zh: 对，通常市场最后会成为定位的「管家」，一旦定位做完。所以之后他们变成定位警察，因为很多定位的东西会以市场物料的形式出现。所以他们投入进来了。我当营销 VP 时，我就是发起定位那事的人——把大家聚一起做定位。然后我通常是驱动搞定 sales pitch 的人，但那是我跟销售、产品一起干。sales pitch 做完后，看组织大小、有没有销售赋能或内部销售能 babysit 这 pitch，通常我和销售头一起弄「好，这是 pitch，锁死了，在出事逼我们改定位前我们不真改这 pitch。那是我们要重看 pitch 的时候」。所以我们会每季度让代表重新认证 pitch 之类的。那通常是我跟销售头合作。但看你怎么搞。我觉得谁拥有它不重要。如果你有个好的产品营销组织，好的产品营销组织一般非常关心定位和 pitch，这两件事在它职责范围内，但看你怎么定义。我等不及你进 Airbnb 了，跟我们讲讲这东西怎么运作。他们不同，因为是消费者，但公司排列各异。所以有产品营销，是一种样；没有，是另一种样。但得有人当这东西的 owner。我们得决定那是谁。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just a couple more questions. One is to motivate people to do this. What kind of impact have you seen at companies that invest this time and rethink the way they pitch?
turns.zh: 就几个问题了。一个是激励人们去做这个。你看到投资这段时间、重新想怎么 pitch 的公司，产生了什么影响？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Well, so people don't like me to talk about revenue stuff. Hugely what we've seen though is again, the immediate impact is felted sales, and everybody's very jazzed about that.
turns.zh: 嗯，人们不喜欢我聊收入那种事。但我们看到的，巨大影响是在销售——立即可感的影响在销售，每个人都超兴奋。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Impact is felt in sales, and everybody's very jazzed about that. Because sometimes what the worry is, is we've got this old positioning and they came in through the pipeline that way. So they were exposed to our marketing somewhere with this old positioning, and then we hit them with the new positioning with this sales pitch. And aren't they going to be all like, "Oh, you moved my cheese." And usually it ends up not being a problem at all. So usually what we see immediately is an uptick in what's happening in sales. And so I've had a couple of companies tell me they've doubled the number of deals that they're bringing from first sales call to opportunity just by tightening up the pitch and getting that going. I think that's not unusual. I worked at a company where we did it in-house where I was the VP marketing, and we, within two quarters, had doubled the revenue just by tightening up the pitch. Just tighten it up.
turns.zh: 影响感在销售，每个人都超兴奋。因为有时担心的是，我们有老定位，他们是从老定位的管道进来的——他们在某处被我们老定位的市场物料触达，然后我们用新定位和新 sales pitch 撞他们。他们不会「哦你动了我的奶酪」吗？通常根本不是问题。所以我们通常立刻看到销售里的上升。我有几家公司告诉我，光靠收紧 pitch、让它跑起来，他们从第一通销售电话到机会 (opportunity) 的单子数翻倍了。我觉得这不罕见。我在家公司自己做（我当营销 VP），两个季度内光靠收紧 pitch 就把收入翻倍了。就收紧它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Holy shit. All right.
turns.zh: holy shit。行吧。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Tighten it up.
turns.zh: 收紧它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No big deal.
turns.zh: 没什么大不了的。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So-
turns.zh: 好。所以——

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: It was a big shift in positioning, I'll tell you that. Not small. Most of the time, we're not doing that. Most of the time, it's a tightening. We're not saying, "Oh, we used to be this and now we're this." Most of the time, it's a tightening, but usually the pitches are so bad. I'm telling you they're so bad that there's this low hanging fruit there that if we could improve it even a little bit, it actually has this big impact on how much stuff survives down the pipe.
turns.zh: 我跟你说，那是定位的一大转变。不小。大多数时候我们不做那个。大多数时候是收紧。我们不是说「哦我们以前是这样现在是那样」。大多数时候是收紧，但通常 pitch 烂得要命。我跟你说它们烂得要命，所以有这么多低垂的果实，我们哪怕改善一点点，就对下游能活下来的东西有巨大影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And again, if folks want to go deep into the positioning step, your first book Obviously Awesome, is a great guide, and our first podcast episode goes through this. Plus you have a guest post in my newsletter where you give them a quick start guide. So there's so many tools to help you through this process.
turns.zh: 再说一次，大家想深挖定位这一步，你的第一本书《Obviously Awesome》是好指南，我们的第一集播客过了这个。加上你在我的 newsletter 有篇客座文章，给他们一个快速上手指南。所以有好多工具帮你过这流程。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So many tools.
turns.zh: 好多工具。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other thought I've had in the back of my mind as we've been chatting is a previous guest, Andy Raskin, has a different framework, feels similar, but I know they're different. His framework starts with a shift that's happened in the world, and then here's who's going to win in the shift, here's who's going to lose. And then he goes into why this product is the best. What's your perspective on that approach versus this approach and the big differences?
turns.zh: 另一个我聊的时候在脑子里想的是：之前的嘉宾 Andy Raskin 有个不同的框架，感觉相似，但我知道它们不同。他的框架从一个世界发生的变化开始，然后谁会赢、谁会输，然后进到为什么这产品最好。你对那个方法 vs 这个方法、以及大区别有什么看法？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So the thing with that framework is I do think it works in certain conditions, but again, I think the conditions might be kind of edgy. So there's a couple of things that I think are lacking in that structure for a sales pitch. So the first one is there's actually no concept of differentiated value in that pitch, which for me is a giant miss. So in that pitch, it assumes that new is inherently valuable and old is inherently bad, and sometimes that's true. So sometimes there's just you versus the status quo and the status quo is some terrible old thing, some legacy thing or it's manual processes or something, and you're the only thing out there, then you can get away with that. But most of the time, we don't have that. Most of the time, there's multiple new ways of doing something and you just can't say, "Well, I'm the only new and the rest of you are old and bad." (01:11:55): So usually I've got to thread the needle. And so that's the first thing. The second thing is that for most companies, if we really understood customer and decision, old is good, it's safe, it's not risky. And does anybody ever say, "No, I'm not going to buy Salesforce. That's the old stuff,"? I just don't think that happens. So in a lot of cases, I don't think you can rely, it's lazy to say, "Buy this because it's new and new is better." Most of the time, the customers are going to want to know, well, what's better about it? Tell me what the value is that I can't get anywhere else. And you're going to have to get more specific than just saying, "Trust me, it's new and new is good." So that's the first thing. The second thing is this idea of starting with a trend. On the surface it looks kind of good, but the problem is often the trend is not unique to you. So everybody else sees the trend too. And so you are starting in a way that any of your competitors could start the same way. (01:12:59): I did this for years where I was taught to do problem solution. We would define the problem like a trend. We'd say, "Well, the change in the world." I was selling databases and I'd say, "Change in the world, data is exponentially growing." It's like, no shit. We all know that. All of my competitors could say that, and all of my competitors deal with the trend in the same way. So unless you have a particularly unique take on the trend, well, then it's not the trend at all really, is it? It's your insight into the trend. So I don't think trend is that great because it's not always unique to you. And ideally what we want is something that we can say that none of our competitors can. And typically a trend is something outside of our control. It's out in the world and everybody else can see it too. (01:13:47): So I don't think it's great. I think that structure looks a lot like the structure we use in a VC pitch or an investor pitch because we're talking about much longer timelines and we can say, "Look, the world is really changing and 10 years from now there's going to be chaos and destruction and the only one standing is us and therefore there is no competition." And because the timeframes are longer and we're talking about disruption of an entire market, which is pretty theoretical, we can get away with a lot of that stuff in investor pitch. In fact, we want to go there in investor pitch. Sales pitch is all about right now. Sales pitch is like, okay, I'm going to exchange my money for right now. You can't get too far into the future. Otherwise, all I'm doing is giving everybody a reason to delay, which they're likely to do anyway because they're indecisive about what they should do.
turns.zh: 那个框架的问题是，我觉得它在某些条件下工作，但那些条件可能有点 edge。我对那个结构作为 sales pitch 有两个缺的东西。第一，那个 pitch 里其实没有「差异化价值」的概念，对我来说是个巨大遗漏。它假设「新」天生有价值、「旧」天生坏，有时那是真的——有时就是你 vs 现状，现状是某个可怕的旧东西、legacy 或手工流程，而你是唯一的新东西，那你混得过去。但大多数时候不是。大多数时候有多种「新」的做法，你不能说「我是唯一的新，你们其他都是旧且坏」。通常我得在针眼里穿线。这是第一点。第二，对大多数公司，如果真理解客户和决策，旧是好的、安全的、不冒险的。有人会说「不，我不买 Salesforce，那是旧东西」吗？我觉得那不会发生。所以很多情况下，你不能依赖「买这个因为它新、新就是更好」——那偷懒。大多数时候客户会想知道「那它好在哪？告诉我那我在别处拿不到的价值」。你得比「信我，它新、新就是好」更具体。这是第一点。第二是「从一个趋势开始」这个点子。表面看不错，但问题是趋势通常不对你独家。别人也看到趋势。所以你起步的方式，任何对手都能用同样的方式起步。我做这个好多年，被教的是「问题-方案」……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like I need a debate version of this podcast where people come on and-
turns.zh: 我感觉我需要这播客出个辩论版，让人上来——

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: I know, but here's the thing that I think people should think about when they're looking at all this stuff because it's terribly confusing if you're trying to figure this out. The one thing I really dislike about the category creation folks is they say that's the only way that you can be successful. And in general, that's just not true about anything. There's lots of ways to do everything. And so I think people should mess around with stuff. And for any of these frameworks, I think they should look at it and see if it works for them and their situation. And maybe it does, maybe it doesn't. (01:15:16): And I think they should steal things from wherever they can steal it and figure out what works in their own situation. My stuff, I like to think is a starting point, folks should use it as a starting point, but people shouldn't be slaves to it. There are lots of things that work at a market, and I think the only thing that we know for certain is that we can't say, "Well, this is the rule and it always works like this." If it was that easy, again, this wouldn't be so hard. We wouldn't have podcasts and newsletters and all kinds of things trying to figure this stuff out.
turns.zh: 我知道，但人们看所有这些时该想的一件事——因为如果你想搞明白会极其困惑——我最不喜欢的品类创造那帮人的一点是，他们说那是你成功的唯一方式。而总体上，对任何事那都不真。每件事都有很多种做法。所以我觉得人们该去试各种东西。对任何这些框架，他们该看它、看对自己和自己的情况有没有用。也许有，也许没有。我觉得他们该从任何能偷的地方偷，搞清楚在自己情况里什么有用。我的东西，我喜欢想成是个起点，人们该当起点用，但不该当奴隶。市场上有很多有用的东西，我们唯一确定知道的是，我们不能说「哦这是规则、永远这样工作」。如果那么容易， again，这也不会这么难。我们不会有播客、newsletter 和一堆东西试图搞明白这些。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Extremely true. Well, with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 极其正确。好，那我们到超刺激的快问快答了。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Oh yeah. Lightning round. Oh gosh. It gives me stress. Okay.
turns.zh: 哦对。快问快答。哦天，给我压力。行吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, question number one. What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Well, that's an easy question. So right now I'm really into Matt Dixon's work right now, which we've mentioned him a couple of times on the podcast, but Matt Dixon's new book called The JOLT Effect is really great just because there's all this data and the things that he discovered with that data, a lot of it go against what we would consider accepted sales wisdom. And so I think that book is full of juicy nuggets and everybody should look at it. His previous book, The Challenger Sale, and there was a companion book to that called The Challenger Customer. Those were also excellent and based on a deep set of research. And those books are older now, but what we see in The JOLT Effect is all the stuff holds true. All the stuff from The Challenger Sale has not changed in 10 years. So I think those books together are really cool. (01:16:54): The other one that I always recommend is the original book on positioning, which is the book by Ries and Trout Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind. I have my copy of it, is dogeared. I probably read that book 100 times and I still see stuff in that book that I didn't see before. So I think if you really want to go deep on this positioning stuff, my book is the how to book. Their book is what is it in the first place book. And I think everybody that's interested in positioning should go read that.
turns.zh: 嗯，那问题简单。现在我真的很迷 Matt Dixon 的作品，我们这集提过他几次，但他的新书《The JOLT Effect》真的很好，因为里面全是数据，而他拿数据发现的很多东西，跟我们以为公认的销售智慧相反。所以我觉得那本书满是 juicy 的洞见，人人都该看。他之前的《The Challenger Sale》，还有本 companion 叫《The Challenger Customer》，也都极好，基于一套深度研究。那些书现在老了，但我们在《The JOLT Effect》里看到，那些东西都成立。《The Challenger Sale》里的东西十年没变。所以我觉得这些书放一起真酷。另一本我总推荐的是定位的原典——Ries 和 Trout 的《Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind》。我的那本都翻烂了。我大概读了 100 遍，还能看到以前没看到的东西。所以如果想深挖定位，我的书是「怎么做」的书，他们的书是「这到底是个啥」的书。我觉得所有对定位感兴趣的人都该去读那本。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. By the way, I have your first book somewhere behind me there. I don't know where it is, but it's there.
turns.zh: 太棒了。顺便，我身后某处也有你的第一本书。我不知道在哪，但在那。

turns.en: I got mine right here so I can do this gag. There it is.
turns.zh: 我这本就在这，所以我才能玩这个梗。在那儿呢。

turns.en: Nailed it.
turns.zh: 漂亮。

turns.en: There's the new one, there's the old one.

turns.en: The YouTube audience can see that trick that you've learned. Second question, what is a favorite recent movie or TV show that you've really enjoyed?

turns.en: So [inaudible 01:17:48] before Parasite, there was this book called, this movie called Snow Piercer. It's really old. I think it came out in-

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've seen that. Is that with the train?
turns.zh: 我看过。是那个火车上的吗？

turns.zh: 2013 年的。你看过吗？

And then we all had to go watch Snow Piercer again. Like me and my daughter watching Snow Piercer. We're really into this movie. turns.zh: 我太爱这部电影了。最近我跟爸去坐火车旅行，出发前我们聊火车。然后我们全得再看一遍《Snow Piercer》。我和我女儿看《Snow Piercer》，我们超迷这部。好笑的是，它刚出时我在家创业公司，CEO 来问「最近看了啥好电影？」我说「哦老天，你一定得看《Snow Piercer》」。他拿去跟一女的约会，第二天回来气疯了。不是有点气，是真的很气我。他说「那是我看过最烂的电影」。我说「哥们，你该告诉我你要去约会，我不知道啊」。

turns.zh: 哦对。

turns.en: All right. Okay, cool. That's two movies for people to watch. I'm curious how people think of Snow Piercer.
turns.zh: 好。酷。那是两部给人看的电影了。我好奇人们怎么看《Snow Piercer》。

turns.zh: 警告：别拿它去约会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man, I still think about that movie sometimes. Next question, what is a favorite interview question you like to ask people that you're interviewing? Usually this is for when you're hiring, so whatever this comes up for you.
turns.zh: 哦老天，我有时还想起那电影。下一个问题，你面试时喜欢问什么最喜欢的面试问题？通常是招聘时用，whatever 对你适用。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So back when I was running teams internally back in my VP marketing days, I felt like a lot of marketing folks came with a certain amount of bad habits, particularly startup marketing folks. It's a bit of the wild west in marketing. And so sometimes they'd come in and you get into somebody new and they'd be really smart, but they learned something at the previous company that you're like, please never do that here. It's not going to work here. And so I developed a thing where I was just looking for attitude. Were you enthusiastic? Are you super into what we're doing here? And I can teach you pretty much anything. The only thing I can't teach you is persuasive writing. And I think that's a learnable skill. I think people can learn how to do persuasive writing. (01:20:12): I just don't have time to teach it to you myself. And so I used to give people a writing test, so I'd say, "Look, think of something you bought recently and write me two paragraphs and just sell me on it." And I used to love that test because people could either do it or they can't. And there's just so much stuff we end up doing in product marketing and marketing that involves a little bit of writing that it's kind of a foundational skill. And if you don't have that, that was the one thing I couldn't teach you.
turns.zh: 我当年在内部带团队、当营销 VP 时，觉得很多营销人带着某些坏习惯来，尤其创业公司营销人。营销有点西部荒野。有时新人进来，很聪明，但在上家公司学了些你「求你别在这做、这不会成」的东西。所以我搞了个东西，只找态度。你热情吗？你对我们在这做的超投入吗？别的我基本都能教你。唯一我教不了的是说服性写作。我觉得那是个可学的技能，人能学会。只是我自己没时间教你。所以我以前给人写作测试：「想个你最近买的东西，写两段，把我卖给它」。我超爱那个测试，因为人会就是会、不会就是不会。产品营销和营销里太多事涉及一点写作，所以它是个基础技能。没有它，那是我唯一教不了你的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that is fascinating. I've never heard of that as an interview question. And I love it. I feel like product managers-
turns.zh: 哇，太有意思了。我从没听过这当面试问题。我超爱。我觉得产品经理——

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: I stole it from a company that made me do it before I got hired, and I was like, this is a really smart thing. I'm [inaudible 01:20:53] stealing it. My thing was I got anxiety and I couldn't decide what product to write about, and I had literally just bought a new pair of running shoes. So I wrote two paragraphs about my new Brooks distance running shoes. But it was good. I got the job.
turns.zh: 我从一家逼我做的公司偷来的，我当时想「这真聪明，我偷了」。我的事是，我当时焦虑、决定不了写啥产品，刚买了双新跑鞋。所以我写了两段关于我的新 Brooks 距离跑鞋。但写得好。我拿到了 offer。

turns.zh: 这完美接上我们的下一个问题：最近有发现什么特别喜欢的产品吗？

turns.zh: 现在我有点迷——我都不知道怎么描述这类东西——就是那种低科技但超棒的东西。我最近超爱的一类是钢笔 (fountain pens)。你写过钢笔吗？

It may be expensive for a pen, but it's not so much money that you wouldn't feel bad if you lost it. So Lamy AL-Star. That's my great product lately. I don't have one right here. And then if you haven't written with a fountain pen, it takes a minute to get used to it, but then it's like, gosh, it just feels great. You'll never write with a ballpoint pen again.
turns.zh: 有家公司 Lamy，在德国，做世界上最好的钢笔。美、惊艳。有些很贵。你想在笔上花很多钱也行。但他们有个叫 AL-Star 的，不贵，20、30 美元。对一支笔可能算贵，但不贵到你丢了会心疼。所以 Lamy AL-Star，那是我最近的大爱产品。我手边没有一支，该拿它当道具的，但我包不在这、它在包里。但 Lamy AL-Star，你谷歌一下，这些笔超美。如果你没写过钢笔，要适应一会，但然后就「天，手感太好了，你再也不想用圆珠笔了」。

turns.zh: 我正想问，是你超享受的那种书写的手感吗？

turns.en: Feel. Totally different. Yeah. Amazing.
turns.zh: 手感。完全不同。对。惊艳。

turns.zh: 我用 Muji 的笔。你知道这些笔吗？

turns.en: Oh yeah, these are actually really good. They're like roller ball pens, roller ball pen, very good, but not as good as the fountain pen.
turns.zh: 哦对，这些其实很好。像滚珠笔，很好，但不如钢笔好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's no fountain pen.
turns.zh: 不是钢笔。

turns.en: The Muji pen is pretty good.
turns.zh: Muji 笔挺好。

turns.en: Then do you have to dip it in ink and stuff? How does that work?

That would be crazy. I can't take that on the airplane, man.
turns.zh: 不。它们要么带个小墨囊你插进去，要么如果你在意环境、不想老扔墨囊，有可 refill 的墨囊，你基本插另一个、它吸进去，对，你不用蘸墨水。那才疯了。我没法带上飞机，哥们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Confiscate your ink. All right, questions get a little more challenging potentially or really easy. Do you have a favorite life motto that you like to repeat to yourself, you like to share with people, that you find useful to come back to?
turns.zh: 没收你的墨水。好，问题可能变难一点、或真的简单。你有没有喜欢的人生格言，常对自己重复、愿意分享给别人、觉得有用会回到的？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: My thing lately is, and maybe this is just an old person thing, but my thing lately is nothing's a big deal. Nothing's a big deal, nothing's a big deal. And so you'll have stuff that you think is a really big deal, positive or negative, and you'll be like, wow, if this thing happened, it'd be so great, and then it happens and you're like, yeah, it's pretty great, but things are good otherwise, or it'll be the opposite. Like, oh, if this thing happened, it'd be so bad. Then it happens and you're like, that wasn't that bad. And so I don't know if this is good or bad, but lately I'm in this zone of I'm in this kind of chill zone where I'm like, nothing's a big deal, man. Everything's cool.
turns.zh: 我最近的东西是——也许这只是老人的事——我最近是「没啥大事」(nothing's a big deal)。没啥大事，没啥大事。所以你会有觉得真是大事的事，好的或坏的，你会「哇如果这发生该多好」，然后它发生了你「嗯，是挺好，但别的也还好」；或者反过来，「哦如果这发生该多糟」，然后它发生了你「也没那么糟」。所以我不知道这好还是坏，但我最近在这个 zone 里——挺 chill 的 zone，我想「没啥大事，哥们，一切都酷」。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That super resonates. And as much as you say that to yourself, it's still hard to convince yourself of that sometimes. But that is a really good motto. I'm going to steal that myself. I kind of say that to myself often in different way.
turns.zh: 那超有共鸣。而且你跟自己这么说，有时还是很难说服自己。但那真是个好格言。我自己也要偷来用。我常用不同方式跟自己说这个。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is the most valuable lesson your mom or your dad taught you?
turns.zh: 你爸妈教过你最有价值的功课是什么？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Yeah, it is funny because it's a little bit related to that. So my dad ran a business, so I grew up in a really small town and my dad and it's cottage country in Canada. And so my dad ran the local toys for tourists, like boats and motorcycles and ATVs and that sort of thing. And he ran that business for years and years and he sold it a few years back when he retired. But it's a neat thing to grow up in entrepreneurial family because you kind of see this highs and lows. The business is really good. Then the business was really bad and then we were all broke and then the business was good and we were not broke. So there was this thing, and my dad used to always kind of have this attitude of you just got to grind it out. (01:25:01): You're just going to grind it out. There's going to be good stuff, there's going to be bad stuff, but the key is to just keep going, just keep going. And so he ran that business for whatever, 30, 40 years. I don't know. His motto is the home of fun since '71. So he started it in '71. I think he sold it three, four years ago. So a long time.
turns.zh: 嗯，好笑的是，这跟那个有点关系。我爸开过公司。我在加拿大一个超小的镇长大，cottage country。我爸做游客的玩具生意——船、摩托、ATV 之类的。他经营很多年，几年前退休时卖了。但在创业家庭长大很妙，因为你能看到高低起伏。生意很好，然后很差、我们全穷了，然后生意好、我们不穷了。所以有这事，我爸总摆出一种态度：你就得硬扛 (grind it out)。好事的、坏事的，但关键是继续走、继续走。所以他经营那生意，whatever，30、40 年。我不知道。他的格言是「自 71 年以来的乐趣之家」(the home of fun since '71)。他 71 年开的，我想三四年前卖的。所以很久。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: It all worked out good in the end. And so I don't know, I think there's something cool about growing up in a family where you can see the highs and lows and then again be like everything's we're just grinding it out over here. Nothing's a big deal.
turns.zh: 最后都好。所以我不知道，我觉得在能看到高低起伏的家庭长大、然后又「我们就是在这硬扛，没啥大事」，有某种酷的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's clear where all that comes from now.
turns.zh: 现在清楚了，这些都从哪来。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question. You do a lot of traveling, you do a lot of speaking, you go to a bunch of cities. I'm curious just what is your favorite either city that you go to that maybe people may not know about or venue that you speak at?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。你旅行很多、演讲很多、去很多城市。我好奇你最喜欢的城市——也许是人们不知道的——或你演讲过的场馆？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: It's such a cliche, but I love Paris. I just love it. But for me, Paris is like a particular vibe. So when I was in university, I did an exchange when I was in engineering and I did third year engineering at a school just outside of Paris. And so I spent the whole year there, learned a bit of French. My French was pretty good at the end. My French is really bad now. So I kind of get Paris. I like Paris. And so when I go to Paris, I just have the best time. I have my set of restaurants I want to go to. I have my handful of places I want to go shopping. I put my butt down in a cafe, look at the beautiful people, drink my nice coffee. I just really dig the whole vibe of Paris and people are starting to know that now. So French companies will call me and they'll say, "Do we get a Paris discount? We hear you like coming here." And I go, "Okay."
turns.zh: 这俗套，但我爱巴黎。我就是爱。对我，巴黎有种特别的 vibe。我大学时，工程系做了个交换，在巴黎郊外一个学校读大三工程。所以我在那待了一整年，学了点法语。最后法语挺好，现在法语超烂。所以我算懂巴黎。我喜欢巴黎。去巴黎时我玩得最开心。我有想去的餐厅清单、想逛的几个地方。我把屁股搁在咖啡馆，看漂亮的人，喝我的好咖啡。我真的 dig 巴黎整个 vibe，现在人们开始知道了。所以法国公司会打电话来「我们有巴黎折扣吗？听说你喜欢来这」。我说「行」。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Now this is going to [inaudible 01:26:51]
turns.zh: 现在这要——

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: There's a great product management conference there called La Product Conference run by these folks at Tega, shout out to Tega. So I've been there a number of times for their conferences and they do an amazing job and the venue is really great. It changes around. But last year, the last time I went there, which was two years ago, it was at an old theater in [inaudible 01:27:13]. Absolutely beautiful. And that was a pretty great venue in a great city with a great conference. So yeah, shout out to French people.
turns.zh: 那有个很棒的产品管理大会叫 La Product Conference，Tega 那帮人办的， shout out 给 Tega。我去过他们大会好几次，他们做得超棒，场馆也很好，会换。但去年——我上次去是两年前——在一个老剧院，绝美。那是个好场馆、好城市、好大会。所以 shout out 给法国人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man. That sounds dreamy. Paris. I see how that could be a favorite. April, I think we accomplished everything we were hoping to accomplish. I think everyone that has listened to this podcast is going to be better at pitching and selling. It feels like even if they take one element of this framework, say starting with an insight or focusing on different value will make them better. And so I'm proud of us. Thank you so much for doing this. Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to reach out and how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 哦老天。听起来像梦。巴黎。我懂它为啥能是最爱。April，我觉得我们完成了希望完成的一切。我觉得每个听这播客的人都会更会 pitch 和卖。感觉哪怕他们只拿这框架的一个元素——比如从洞察开始、或聚焦不同价值——都会让他们更好。所以我为我们骄傲。太感谢你做这个。最后两个问题。人们想联系你能在哪找到你在线，以及听众能怎么帮到你？

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: So where can people find me? I'm aprildunford.com. The only social media I'm doing these days is LinkedIn. I'm a bit social media-ed out. I'm experimenting a little on threads and Instagram, but LinkedIn is a good place to find me if you just want low lift way to follow my stuff. But I'm doing all the things now, Lenny, I got a podcast, it's called Positioning with April Dunford. I got a newsletter that's also called Positioning. You can find that if you go to, it's on Substacks, you can find it there, otherwise aprildunford.com/books and you can sign up there. But those are the big things. And then there's the books, obviously, if you want to learn more about this stuff. Everything I know is in the book. There isn't stuff that I know that isn't in the book to be honest.
turns.zh: 人们能在哪找到我？aprildunford.com。我最近唯一用的社交媒体是 LinkedIn，我有点社媒疲了。我在 threads 和 Instagram 稍微试一下，但 LinkedIn 是个低负担跟我的好地方。但我现在啥都做，Lenny，我有个播客叫《Positioning with April Dunford》。我有个 newsletter 也叫 Positioning，在 Substack 上能找到，不然去 aprildunford.com/books 能注册。但那些是大头。然后有书，显然，想学更多就看书。我知道的都在书里，老实说没有书里没有的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. And then how can listeners be useful to you? Just check out those things.
turns.zh: 太棒了。那听众能怎么帮到你？就去看看那些东西。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: I guess so. You know what? I'm in this phase. I think, again, I think it's an old age thing. I am in this kind of philosophical phase where I'm not going to be doing this forever. And what I'm trying to do right now is get everything that's useful out of my head and out in the world before I'm done. And so right now I'm very focused on delivering useful things for other people. I didn't think I needed to write a book about sales pitches, but then I got the idea in my head, everybody's sales pitch is so bad and there isn't a book on how to build a sales pitch. And I'm not saying mine's the world's greatest thing, but it's better than nothing. So this is what I'm trying to do right now. I'm trying to be useful to other people because pretty soon I'm not going to be doing anything, I think is the idea.
turns.zh: 我想是吧。你知道吗，我在这个阶段。我觉得，again，是老的事。我在这个有点哲学的 phase，我不会永远做这个。我现在想做的，是在收工前把我脑子里有用的东西全倒出来、放到世界上。所以现在我非常聚焦在给别人的有用的东西。我本来不觉得需要写本关于 sales pitch 的书，但后来脑子里有了个点子：每个人的 sales pitch 都这么烂，而居然没有一本讲怎么建 sales pitch 的书。我不是说我的书是世界最牛的，但比没有强。所以这是我现在想做的。我想对别人有用，因为很快我大概就不做这些了，我想是这意思。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Arnold Schwarzenegger's new book is called Be Useful. And I feel like that's the perfect description of how to be successful and especially in the work that we do, just helping people. But I keep coming back to that. It's just be useful.
turns.zh: Arnold Schwarzenegger 的新书叫《Be Useful》（做个有用的人）。我觉得那是对怎么成功的完美描述，尤其在我们做的这工作里，就是帮人。但我一直回到那。就是 be useful。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: I think this is a really important thing. When I wrote the first book, people started writing back to me and saying, "Oh, your book was so great." And my reflex action was to say, "Oh, I'm glad you enjoyed it." But then I stumped myself and I was like, you know what? I don't actually care if you enjoyed it. This isn't entertainment. I'm actually trying to create something that's useful. So what I really want is for people to read this stuff and come back and say, "That was useful. We were struggling with this thing, and that unlocked something for me and that was useful." And that's what I'm trying to do right now.
turns.zh: 我觉得这是很重要的事。我写第一本书时，人们写回来说「哦你的书太棒了」。我的反射动作是「哦很高兴你喜欢」。但我卡了一下，想「你知道吗？我其实不在乎你喜不喜欢。这不是娱乐。我其实在创造有用的东西」。所以我真想要的是人们读这些、回来说「那有用。我们卡在这事上，那帮我解锁了点什么，那有用」。这就是我现在想做的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: April, thank you so much for being here. This was amazing.
turns.zh: April，太感谢你来了。这太棒了。

turns.speaker: April Dunford
turns.en: Thanks so much. It's always good to be here.
turns.zh: 太感谢。能来总是好。

turns.en: Always good to have you here. And we might do a V3 when you do a third book if you ever-
turns.zh: 能请你来总是好。如果你出第三本书，我们可能做 V3——如果 ever——

turns.en: No, not happening.
